---
title: "Signed and absolute gender-gap targets"
subtitle: "5.6 · after the postrank theory book, chapters 4 and 20; KRW’s gender data"
description: "Target-specific posterior probabilities and fixed-order reports for signed and absolute contact gaps."
---

A signed male-name contact advantage and its absolute magnitude are distinct reporting targets. A large female-name
advantage is low on the signed scale but large on the absolute scale. Each target has its own released posterior
pair probabilities, expected-rank order and optimal cuts within that order. The display compares the resulting
relations and marginal summaries for all firms. Folding a posterior distribution also differs from taking the
absolute value of its mean. Consequently, the absolute-target report cannot be recovered from the signed means or
direction probabilities alone.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Both target-specific cards.** Both computations use at most 4 grades at withholding cost τ .20. The family label beside each result specifies that each is labelled “optimal within this order.” The two orders can differ,
  so neither result is a certificate of optimality over every possible report.
- **Every changed pair.** The “Complete list of changed unordered pairs” keeps every relation that changes from the signed report to the absolute
  report. A direction can appear, disappear or reverse. Each row names both firms and shows the wrong-direction
  probability under the law for that report. These are different targets, so their risk values are not a
  comparison under one fixed loss.
- **All firm summaries.** “All firms in released ID order” keeps all 97 firms together. The table keeps the supplied means and
  central 90% intervals for both targets, their expected ranks and their chosen grades. A folded posterior mean
  is not obtained by taking the absolute value of a signed posterior mean.

The report cards use supplied marginal intervals only to describe individual firms. Their grades come from
pair probabilities, the declared order, the cap and the withholding cost. Sharing a grade states no direction;
it does not assert equality. The folded probabilities come directly from the public postrank data object’s
absolute-gender alternative. The app does not refit independent normal distributions to those summaries or infer
a joint race–gender posterior from marginal information.

Both precision views keep the signed gender estimate’s original sampling SE. Beside the folded report, it is
only a precision covariate, not an SE of the absolute target. A shared middle grade is not evidence of average behavior.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The two reports are newly computed cuts of their own expected-rank orders. They are not KRW’s archived cards.
